plan.angle: Slide 1: 'Plague has 3 forms. Only one, pneumonic, usually spreads person to person (CDC, WHO).' Slides 2–7 as planned. Keep CDC incubation figures together on slide 7 (bubonic 2–8 days, pneumonic 1–3 days), tagged CDC. plan.why: 'What is pneumonic plague' searches spiked with the story. A comparison that names all 3 forms is a durable resource people save, whatever the final diagnosis turns out to be. | fact-check: The framework is sound and the 3 forms are standard (CDC, WHO). Fixes: (1) The hook line 'Russian authorities say no plague found in the Irkutsk case' is a scope error. The 'no pathogens found' result applies to the contacts tested. For the case itself, Russia says the death was 'pneumonia of undetermined origin' and that no plague case has been recorded, while WHO says lab testing on the cause of death continues. A carousel is static, so keep that line off slide 1. Put a dated status line on the final slide, or drop it. (2) Incubation figures differ by source. CDC says 2–8 days for bubonic and 1–3 days for pneumonic. WHO says 1–7 days overall, and as short as about 24 hours for pneumonic. Quote one source per slide with its tag and don't mix them. (3) Septicemic plague can start on its own or develop from untreated bubonic plague, and both can lead to secondary pneumonic plague. So slide 1 should say 'usually spreads', and the table should note that the other forms can become pneumonic. (4) Slide 8 must not name drugs or doses. (5) No graphic imagery: no images of buboes, gangrene or blackened fingers.

CDC: plague comes in 3 forms, and only one usually spreads person to person.

Swipe to see:
→ Bubonic: painful swollen lymph nodes, usually from a flea bite, not usually contagious
→ Septicemic: bloodstream infection, extreme weakness, shock
→ Pneumonic: fast-moving pneumonia, and the only form that can spread between people through close contact (CDC)

Sudden fever with painful swollen lymph nodes, or cough and chest pain, after possible exposure (flea bites or sick animals in a plague area, or close contact with a suspected case)? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

social.facebook_caption:
Plague actually comes in 3 forms, and they're not all the same when it comes to spreading between people.

Bubonic plague (painful swollen lymph nodes) and septicemic plague (bloodstream infection) usually don't spread person to person. They mostly come from infected flea bites or from handling infected animals. Pneumonic plague is different: it affects the lungs and can spread through close contact with respiratory droplets, according to the CDC.

The CDC says that in recent decades the US has averaged about 7 human plague cases a year (range 0–17), mostly in the rural western US, and over 80% of them have been bubonic. The good news: all 3 forms are treatable. WHO says antibiotics are effective if plague is diagnosed in time, and CDC says treatment should start as soon as plague is suspected.

If someone has a sudden fever with painful swollen lymph nodes, or sudden cough and chest pain, after possible exposure (flea bites or sick animals in a plague area, or close contact with a suspected case), they should contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Did you know plague had 3 different forms? Let us know in the comments.

factcheck.summary: I checked every factual claim against the 5 cited sources and each one supports what the carousel says. CDC Symptoms (reviewed 15 May 2024) gives the symptoms for each form, the incubation figures (bubonic 2–8 days, pneumonic as short as 1 day) and says pneumonic is "the only form of plague that can be spread from person to person". CDC How Plague Spreads supports fleas as the most common route, handling infected animals, and droplets needing "direct and close contact". CDC Maps & Statistics (reviewed 25 Mar 2025) gives an average of 7 cases a year (range 0–17) and says "over 80%" were bubonic. The 8-of-10 pictogram labelled "8+ in 10" doesn't round up. The WHO fact sheet (updated 29 Sep 2026) supports the "recovery rates are high if … treated … within 24 hours" line, says bubonic person-to-person spread is "rare", and says antibiotics work if patients are diagnosed in time. The carousel makes no claims about the Irkutsk case, so no status date is needed. It has the urgent-care line and the "talk to a health professional" line, and it doesn't use fear-bait. There are 4 minor wording fixes for precision: the pneumonic "usual route" cell, the strength of "Yes" in the person-to-person cell, the attribution on the treatment slide, and adding exposure context to the red-flag line.

issues.problem: CDC says pneumonic plague can also develop when untreated bubonic or septicemic plague spreads to the lungs, and in the US that is a common way it arises. Saying inhalation is the 'usual' route overstates it. The note in the slide body already covers the lung-spread route, but the table cell should match it.
issues.fix: Change the Pneumonic value to: "Breathing in droplets, or spread from untreated bubonic/septicemic"

issues.location: Slide 7 (comparison), row 'Person to person?', Pneumonic column
issues.problem: CDC says pneumonic plague 'can' spread and that this requires 'direct and close contact'. A flat 'Yes' sounds stronger than the source, and slide 6 already uses 'can'.
issues.fix: Change the value to: "Can, with direct close contact"

issues.claim: "CDC, WHO: antibiotics work against all 3 forms when started in time."
issues.problem: The WHO fact sheet says this directly. The cited CDC Clinical Care page says to start therapy as soon as plague is suspected, but it doesn't make the 'all 3 forms' statement in so many words. Attribute the claim only to the source that says it.
issues.fix: Change the body to: "WHO: antibiotics are effective against plague if it's diagnosed in time, and pneumonic plague recovery rates are high if treated within 24 hours of symptoms starting. CDC: treatment should start as soon as plague is suspected."

issues.claim: "Sudden fever plus swollen painful lymph nodes, or cough and chest pain? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently."
issues.problem: Fever with swollen glands, or cough with chest pain, is very common and usually not plague. Without exposure context, this line could cause needless alarm. The urgent-care advice is right, but it should be tied to possible exposure.
issues.fix: Change the body to: "Sudden fever with painful swollen lymph nodes, or cough and chest pain, after possible exposure (flea bites or sick animals in a plague area, or close contact with a suspected case)? Contact a doctor or local health authority urgently. If you're worried, talk to a health professional."
